scenes.tts: How do you see the shape of a large protein? X-ray crystallography needs well-ordered crystals. N M R in solution works only for relatively small proteins. Membrane proteins pulled out of the membrane tend to clump. Electron microscopy had three obstacles. The beam burns biological material. A weaker beam gives low contrast. And the vacuum dries out water-soluble molecules.
scenes.visual: One large protein blob with a question mark; a crystal lattice of identical blobs and a small-protein-only tag; membrane proteins pulled out clump; then three obstacle panels: beam burns, faint contrast, dried and collapsed.

scenes.tts: Purify the molecule, because averaging assumes identical particles. Spread a small drop as a thin film on a fine metal mesh grid, blot it, and plunge it into liquid ethane. Cooling this fast turns the water into glass, not crystals. A glass is disordered, so the beam scatters evenly and the background is uniform. The molecules stay in water, not dried or stained.
scenes.visual: Mixed blobs become identical purified blobs; a drop on a mesh grid is blotted to a film and plunged into an ethane bath; crystal lattice ice crossed out, glassy ice with blobs held in it.

scenes.tts: Image the frozen grid. The particles lie in many random orientations, so each image is a flat projection of a different view. Contrast is very low, so images are taken out of focus, and the contrast transfer function is measured per image and corrected. Radiation damage limits the dose.
scenes.visual: Beam passes through the grid; the same blob object is shown in many random orientations and the flat silhouette each gives; images defocus, a curve modulates, a dose limit; movie frames shift back into line.

scenes.tts: Software picks the particle images, aligns them, and sorts similar views into two D classes. Averaging a class gives a sharper picture of one view. Then work out how the views relate in three D, build a starting model, and refine it against the particle images. If the data hold more than one shape, sort the particles into separate three D classes.
scenes.visual: Noisy particle images are boxed, sorted into class bins, averaged into sharper pictures; class views arranged around a contour map; the map refines; a mixed set splits into two contour maps.
scenes.caption: Software picks the particle images, aligns them, and sorts similar views into 2D classes. Averaging a class gives a sharper picture of one view. Then work out how the views relate in 3D, build a starting model, and refine it against the particle images. If the data hold more than one shape, sort the particles into separate 3D classes.
scenes.narration: Software picks the particle images, aligns them, and sorts similar views into 2D classes. Averaging a class gives a sharper picture of one view. Then work out how the views relate in 3D, build a starting model, and refine it against the particle images. If the data hold more than one shape, sort the particles into separate 3D classes.

scenes.tts: The raw micrograph shows each particle as a faint, noisy shape against grey ice. A class average sums many aligned images of one view, so noise falls and features appear. The final output is a three D map with a stated resolution, estimated by splitting the data in two and measuring how well the halves agree. The reported resolution is a broad guideline, not a firm number.
scenes.visual: Example micrograph of faint particles; an average of many aligned images sharpens; half maps and an idealised agreement curve with a cutoff line; resolution marked as a band.

scenes.tts: Overfitting: aligning noise can create features and inflate the resolution. The control is to refine halves of the data independently. In one tomography survey, about ninety percent of particles stuck to an air-water interface. That can denature protein and cause preferred orientations, which means too few views. Thicker ice, a little detergent, or a thin support film can help, but thicker ice and most support films cost contrast.
scenes.visual: Noise aligned into a fake feature, the two independent halves disagree; particles pinned at the surface of the ice show one view only, with three remedies each costing contrast.

scenes.tts: Mouse Piezo one is a membrane protein. In 2017, Guo and MacKinnon showed the closed trimer at three point seven angstroms as a curved, three-bladed propeller. In detergent, the micelle forms a dome. They proposed that in a membrane, tension changes gating energetics in proportion to the change in projected area under the dome.
scenes.visual: Membrane with a domed three-blade protein outline; area under the dome; vesicle particles sorted into curved and flat classes; a note that the steps are not claimed.

scenes.tts: In 2022, Jeong, Clark, Gouaux and colleagues solved the native C. elegans TMC-1 complex, a worm structure, not mammalian. It holds two copies each of TMC-1, CALM-1 and TMIE, and a subset also carried ARRD-6. Particles from a native extract could be sorted by computer into complexes with and without it. A structure is a static reconstruction of purified protein. It is not a time course or a recording of function. Pair it with electrophysiology or mutants.
scenes.visual: Native extract particles sorted into two classes, with and without a fourth chip; counts of copies; closing contrast of a still map against a trace.
